name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Comparison of bond angles in alcohol and ether

questiontext.text:
The structural representations and bond angles of methanol and methoxymethane are shown in the diagram below:

Which of the following statements correctly explains why the \(\mathrm{C-O-C}\) bond angle in methoxymethane (\(111.7^\circ\)) is significantly larger than the tetrahedral angle (\(109.5^\circ\)) and the \(\mathrm{C-O-H}\) bond angle in methanol (\(108.9^\circ\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Structural Features
The central oxygen atom in both methanol (\(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\)) and methoxymethane (\(\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}\)) is \(sp^3\) hybridised, possessing two bonding pairs and two lone pairs of electrons. In methanol, the \(\mathrm{C-O-H}\) bond angle is \(108.9^\circ\), whereas in methoxymethane, the \(\mathrm{C-O-C}\) bond angle is \(111.7^\circ\).

Step 2: Electronic Repulsions in Methanol
In methanol, due to the presence of two unshared electron pairs (lone pairs) on the oxygen atom, strong lone pair-lone pair and lone pair-bond pair repulsions push the two single bonds closer together, causing the bond angle to decrease slightly from the regular tetrahedral value of \(109.5^\circ\) to \(108.9^\circ\).

Step 3: Steric Repulsion in Methoxymethane
In methoxymethane, oxygen is bonded to two bulky methyl (\(-\mathrm{CH_3}\)) groups instead of hydrogen atoms. The strong repulsive interaction between these two bulky alkyl groups overcomes the lone-pair compressional effect, forcing the \(\mathrm{C-O-C}\) bond angle to open up to \(111.7^\circ\), which is slightly greater than the tetrahedral angle.

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
The primary factor widening the \(\mathrm{C-O-C}\) bond angle beyond tetrahedral geometry in ethers is the steric repulsion between the two bulky alkyl groups attached to the central oxygen atom.

answer.text: Steric repulsive interactions between the two bulky methyl groups attached to the oxygen atom
Stronger lone pair-lone pair repulsion on the oxygen atom in the ether molecule
Greater electronegativity of the methyl carbon compared to hydrogen
Presence of extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding in methoxymethane

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Intermediate and byproduct in cumene phenol synthesis

questiontext.text:
The industrial manufacture of phenol from cumene (isopropylbenzene) proceeds according to the reaction sequence shown below:

Identify the chemical structures or names of intermediate [X] and by-product [Y] produced in this commercial process.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reaction Sequence
The scheme shows the conversion of cumene (isopropylbenzene) into phenol via intermediate [X] upon oxidation with oxygen (\(\mathrm{O_2}\)), followed by acid-catalysed hydrolysis (\(\mathrm{H^+/H_2O}\)) to yield phenol and an organic by-product [Y].

Step 2: Identification of Intermediate [X]
When cumene is oxidised in the presence of air or oxygen, the tertiary benzylic \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond is converted into a hydroperoxide group. The resulting intermediate is cumene hydroperoxide, having the chemical structure \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C(CH_3)_2-O-O-H}\).

Step 3: Cleavage to Phenol and By-product [Y]
Subsequent treatment of cumene hydroperoxide with dilute acid causes a rearrangement and cleavage reaction. The phenyl group migrates to oxygen with loss of water, forming a hemiacetal-like species that decomposes into phenol (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\)) and propan-2-one (acetone, \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)).

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
Intermediate [X] is cumene hydroperoxide and by-product [Y] is acetone (propan-2-one), which is an important and valuable commercial byproduct of this industrial route.

answer.text: Intermediate [X] is cumene hydroperoxide, and by-product [Y] is acetone (propan-2-one)
Intermediate [X] is 2-phenylpropan-2-ol, and by-product [Y] is acetaldehyde (ethanal)
Intermediate [X] is cumene hydroperoxide, and by-product [Y] is propan-2-ol
Intermediate [X] is acetophenone, and by-product [Y] is methanol

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Chemoselective reduction of keto-ester with sodium borohydride

questiontext.text:
Consider the chemoselective reduction shown in the chemical scheme below:

What is the structure of the major organic product [P] formed in this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Functional Groups
The starting reactant is methyl 2-(2-oxocyclohexyl)acetate (or methyl (2-oxocyclohexyl)ethanoate). It contains two distinct carbonyl-containing functional groups: 1. A cyclic ketone group on the cyclohexane ring (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)). 2. An ester group (\(-\mathrm{COOCH_3}\)) on the side chain.

Step 2: Reducing Agent and Selectivity
The reagent used is sodium borohydride (\(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\)). Sodium borohydride is a mild and selective hydride reducing agent. It readily reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols, but under ordinary conditions it does not reduce esters, carboxylic acids, or amides.

Step 3: Identification of the Product [P]
Because \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\) specifically reduces the keto carbonyl group while leaving the ester functionality completely unaffected: - The cyclic ring ketone (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)) is reduced to a secondary alcohol group (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)). - The side-chain ester group (\(-\mathrm{CH_2COOCH_3}\)) remains unchanged. Thus, the major product [P] is methyl 2-(2-hydroxycyclohexyl)acetate.

Step 4: Check and Final Conclusion
The reaction yields methyl 2-(2-hydroxycyclohexyl)acetate, wherein only the keto carbonyl group on the cyclohexane ring is reduced to a hydroxyl group, leaving the ester intact.

answer.text: Methyl 2-(2-hydroxycyclohexyl)acetate, where only the ring ketone is reduced to a secondary alcohol
2-(2-Oxocyclohexyl)ethanol, where only the ester group is reduced to an alcohol
2-(2-Hydroxycyclohexyl)ethanol, where both the ketone and the ester groups are reduced to alcohols
2-(2-Oxocyclohexyl)ethanal, where the ester group is partially reduced to an aldehyde

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Identity of the intermediate in Reimer Tiemann reaction

questiontext.text:
The stepwise pathway for the conversion of phenol to salicylaldehyde via the Reimer–Tiemann reaction is outlined below:

What is the nature of the substituent attached to the ortho position of the phenoxide ring in Intermediate [A]?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reimer–Tiemann Reaction Overview
On treating phenol with chloroform (\(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\)) in the presence of aqueous sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)), a \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group is introduced primarily at the ortho position of the benzene ring, producing salicylaldehyde upon final acidification.

Step 2: Generation of Electrophile and Attack
Hydroxide deprotonates chloroform to generate dichlorocarbene (\(:\!\mathrm{CCl_2}\)), which is an electron-deficient electrophile. Concurrently, phenol is converted into the strongly nucleophilic phenoxide ion. Attack of dichlorocarbene on the activated ortho position yields a substituted benzal chloride intermediate.

Step 3: Identity of Intermediate [A]
In Intermediate [A], the phenoxide oxygen exists as \(-\mathrm{O^-Na^+}\), and the group attached at the ortho carbon is a dichloromethyl moiety (\(-\mathrm{CHCl_2}\)). This corresponds to a substituted benzal chloride.

Step 4: Hydrolysis and Acidification
Treatment of Intermediate [A] with sodium hydroxide hydrolyses the geminal dichloride (\(-\mathrm{CHCl_2}\)) into an unstable gem-diol that loses water to yield the sodium salt of salicylaldehyde (Intermediate [B], bearing \(-\mathrm{CHO}\)). Subsequent acidification with \(\mathrm{H^+}\) gives salicylaldehyde.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The substituent present at the ortho position in Intermediate [A] is the dichloromethyl group (\(-\mathrm{CHCl_2}\)).

answer.text: A dichloromethyl group (\(-\mathrm{CHCl_2}\))
A trichloromethyl group (\(-\mathrm{CCl_3}\))
A chloromethyl group (\(-\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\))
A formyl chloride group (\(-\mathrm{COCl}\))

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Carbocation rearrangement during substitution with HBr

questiontext.text:
The reaction of 3-methylbutan-2-ol with concentrated hydrobromic acid (\(\mathrm{HBr}\)) is illustrated below:

Which of the following correctly identifies the major organic product [P] and the rearrangement step responsible for its formation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reactant and Conditions
The reactant is 3-methylbutan-2-ol, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH(OH)-CH_3}\), a secondary alcohol treated with concentrated \(\mathrm{HBr}\).

Step 2: Protonation and Formation of Initial Carbocation
Protonation of the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group produces an alkyloxonium ion, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH(OH_2^+)-CH_3}\). Loss of a water molecule yields an initial secondary (\(2^\circ\)) carbocation: \[\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3}\]

Step 3: Carbocation Rearrangement (1,2-Hydride Shift)
The initial \(2^\circ\) carbocation is adjacent to a tertiary carbon atom bearing a hydrogen atom. A 1,2-hydride (\(\mathrm{H^-}\)) shift from the tertiary carbon (C3) to the positively charged secondary carbon (C2) occurs rapidly, transforming the less stable \(2^\circ\) carbocation into a much more stable tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) carbocation: \[\mathrm{(CH_3)_2\overset{+}{C}-CH_2-CH_3}\]

Step 4: Nucleophilic Attack and Major Product Formation
Nucleophilic attack of the bromide ion (\(\mathrm{Br^-}\)) onto the rearranged \(3^\circ\) carbocation gives 2-bromo-2-methylbutane as the predominant (major) product: \[\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(Br)-CH_2-CH_3}\] Direct attack of bromide on the un-rearranged \(2^\circ\) carbocation would only form 2-bromo-3-methylbutane as a minor product.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, formed via a 1,2-hydride shift from the adjacent tertiary carbon to generate the stable tertiary carbocation.

answer.text: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, via a 1,2-hydride shift to form a stable tertiary carbocation
2-Bromo-3-methylbutane, without any rearrangement via direct nucleophilic attack on the secondary carbocation
1-Bromo-3-methylbutane, via a 1,2-methyl shift to form a primary carbocation
2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, via a 1,2-methyl shift to form a secondary carbocation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_DIAGRAM_Q06 - Mechanism of cleavage of tert butyl methyl ether with HI

questiontext.text:
The mechanism for the cleavage of tert-butyl methyl ether with one equivalent of hydroiodic acid (\(\mathrm{HI}\)) is shown in the reaction scheme below:

Which statement correctly accounts for the products formed and the reaction mechanism operating in this cleavage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reactant and Reagents
The starting substrate is an unsymmetrical ether containing one methyl group and one tertiary alkyl (tert-butyl) group: tert-butyl methyl ether, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-O-CH_3}\), reacting with one equivalent of \(\mathrm{HI}\).

Step 2: Protonation of Ether
In the first step, the ether oxygen is protonated by \(\mathrm{HI}\) to produce the tert-butylmethyloxonium ion, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-\overset{+}{O}(H)-CH_3}\).

Step 3: Mechanism of Bond Cleavage (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\) vs \(\mathrm{S_N2}\))
When an ether contains one primary or methyl group and one tertiary alkyl group, cleavage does not follow an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) pathway. Instead, departure of the neutral leaving group (methanol, \(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\)) occurs in a slow, rate-determining step to generate a highly stable tertiary carbocation, the tert-butyl carbocation \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^+}\). This is an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism.

Step 4: Product Formation
In the subsequent fast step, the iodide ion (\(\mathrm{I^-}\)) attacks the tert-butyl carbocation to yield tert-butyl iodide (\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-I}\)). Methanol remains unchanged when only one equivalent of \(\mathrm{HI}\) is used.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The cleavage proceeds by an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) pathway because departure of methanol produces an exceptionally stable tertiary carbocation, yielding tert-butyl iodide and methanol as the products.

answer.text: The reaction proceeds via an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism because a highly stable tertiary carbocation is formed, yielding tert-butyl iodide and methanol
The reaction proceeds via an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism because iodide attacks the less hindered methyl group, yielding methyl iodide and tert-butyl alcohol
The reaction proceeds via an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism because a stable methyl carbocation is formed, yielding methyl iodide and tert-butyl alcohol
The reaction proceeds via an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism because iodide attacks the tertiary carbon with complete inversion of configuration
